goal: Give the migration drift checker a concept of migration target, so a merged migration whose real target is another database is excluded from the production promotion queue by DERIVED scope rather than by a version skip, and is reported in its own clearly-labelled section instead of vanishing. Record the hts_rag_split migration (20260909121403) under that mechanism, citing issue #2403.
dispatcher: albert autonomous overnight authorization for issue #2820
prohibited_actions: Do not delete, move, or edit the hts_rag_split migration file, and do not hard-code a skip for its version; the gap is that the checker has no concept of target, and a one-off skip leaves the next cross-project migration in the same trap.
Do not create a migration file or claim a migration author lane; this is repo-maintenance, not structural.
Do not let an excluded migration be reported silently; an invisible exclusion is its own hazard and a later reader must be able to see the claim and challenge it.
Do not weaken, bypass, or delete any guard to make a check pass, including the throughput truth audit.
Do not run DDL against any database; this change reads the migration ledger only.
Do not edit C:/repos/shared-db directly; it is landing-only and its checkout restores from a stale index.
assumptions: Migration 20260909121403 targets the DesignFlow non-production Supabase project, not shared production. Confirmed by reading both issue #2403 and the migration's own header, as the issue demanded, rather than assuming it.

An unregistered migration stays in scope for every target, so a forgotten registry entry can only over-report work, never hide it. The mechanism is deliberately fail-safe in the direction the issue called worse than the bug.

The production and preview drift runs read the migration ledger only and need no database credential beyond the Supabase access token, which is injected from the 1Password vault vibe_coding and never appears in arguments or logs.

The two live drift runs are deliberately NOT listed as required_checks. Both exit 1 by design, because real unrelated drift legitimately remains on both targets, and a required check is a command that proves the work by PASSING. They are recorded instead as verbatim probe evidence in the completion report and the pull request, where their exit code and full output are stated rather than hidden. Listing them as gates would have forced a choice between misreporting their exit code and appearing to fail.
stop_conditions: Stop and report if 20260909121403 turns out to be production-scoped after all, because excluding it would hide real work from the promotion queue.
Stop if the exclusion cannot be shown to fail: a known in-scope migration must still be reported as promotable, or the mechanism is indistinguishable from one that swallows everything.
Stop if a guard refusal could only be cleared by weakening the guard rather than by correcting the work.
